cat.name: Domestic Violence
cat.q:
How did the first evidence of parity come out?
The finding was not an invention but discovery of a neglected piece. As early as 1986 there were 23 studies including 2 national surveys that found parity in perpetration (i.e. men and women are equally abusing their partners). By 2010 Murray Straus was one of the first few researchers who summarised 200 studies that found this equal rates.
Around this time one of the founder of Duluth model rejected it: In 1999, Pence even doubted her own model stating '... [the model] did not fit the lived experience of many of the men and women we were working for.... Many of the men I[Pence] interviewed did not seem to articulate a desire for power of their partner. Eventually we realized we were finding what we had already predetermined to find.'

Does the data pattern change by country, sample types, lifetime rates instaead of last 12 months rate and methodology?
1) Data of country: (Percentage of Bilateral: Unilateral female perpetrated: Unilateral male perpetrated): a) United States: 51,35,16 b) Canada: 48:32:30 c) United Kingdom:57,28,17 d) Australia and New Zeeland: 56:22:27 e) Other: 71:19:15
2) Data by sample type:(Percentage of Bilateral: Unilateral female perpetrated: Unilateral male perpetrated): a) Large Population Studies:51,34,18 b) Small Community studies: 49,34,17 c) Middle or high school students: 45,34,13 d) University/college students: 60,27,14 e) Clinical samples: 59,29,22
3) "Our findings indicate remarkable levels of agreement on reporting patterns of both bidirectional and unidirectional violence by men and woman suggesting that the results are likely valid and reliable."
4) This was false too. Change in methodology also did not change the pattern of data significantly
[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/386189016_Bidirectional_and_Unidirectional_Intimate_Partner_Violence_A_Comprehensive_Review]

Are Women's violence caused by self defence?
At least six other studies report data on self-defense. Like the DeKesseredy et al. study, five of the six found that only a small percentage of female violence was in self-defense (Carrado, George, Loxam, Jones, & Templar, 1996; Cascardi & Vivian, 1995; Felson & Messner, 1998; Follingstad, Wright, Lloyd, & Sebastian, 1991; Pearson, 1997; Sarantakos, 1998; Sommer, 1996). For the one study that found high rates of self-defense, the percentage in self defense was slightly greater for men (56%) than for women (42%) (Harned, 2001).
Rather than self-defense, the most usual motivations for violence by women, like the motivations of men, are coercion, anger, and punishing misbehavior by their partner (Cascardi & Vivian, 1995; Fiebert & Gonzalez, 1997). For example, Pearson (1997) reports that 90% of the women she studied assaulted their partner because they were furious or jealous, or frustrated and not because they tried to defend themselves. [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0190740907001855?via%3Dihub]
A study analysed 16k+ 'perpetrators only' sample: it found self-defence as the least of the reasons for dv. And 13% men and 9% women reported this as reason. [https://www.psycnet.org/record/2019-21168-001]

What about WHO's claim that it is indeed self defence?
For example, the influential World Health Organization report on violence states that “Where violence by women occurs it is more likely to be in the form of self-defense (32, 37, 38)” (Krug et al., 2002). However, examination of references 32, 37, and 38 found that although all three asserted that women's violence was primarily in self-defense, #32 Saunders (Saunders, 1986) reported no data on self-defense, #37 DeKesseredy et al. (DeKeseredy, Saunders, Schwartz, & Shahid, 1997) does report data but their data shows that only 6.9% of the women acted in self-defense, and reference #38 Johnson & Ferraro (Michael P. Johnson & Ferraro, 2000) is a review article that cites references 32 and 37 and other references which also present no empirical data. [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0190740907001855?via%3Dihub]

Do men's reason for domestic violence arises from dominance and control?
Motives behind violence: (Percentage of Men:Women) a) Anger: 47:68 b) Retaliation: 28:49 c) Control: 27:35 d) Jealousy: 25:37 e) Gaining Attention: 55:53 f) Inability to express verbally: 36:32 g) Self Defence: 13:9 [https://www.psycnet.org/record/2019-21168-001]
b) Eight studies directly compared men and women in the power/control motive and subjected their findings to statistical analyses. Three reported no significant gender differences and one had mixed findings. One paper found that women were more motivated to perpetrate violence as a result of power/control than were men, and three found that men were more motivated; however, gender differences were weak [https://domesticviolenceresearch.org/]

Many papers cite greater effect of dominance in male violence, why this contradiction?
Another recent example by an experienced and respected researcher is the assertion by Hamberger (Hamberger & Guse, 2002) that “Men in contrast {to women} appear to be motivated to use violence to dominate and control”. Their article cited about 80 studies, but none of them provided empirical evidence on gender differences in dominance and control motivation [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0190740907001855?via%3Dihub]

Are women injured at an extremely disproportionate rate?
Women are injured at a rate higher than men, but the difference is 1/6th of a standard deviation, which is mathematically very small. And women were 62% of all injured people, which is not a very large disparity. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10989615/]
ONS 2023 reports: (Percentage of men : women) a) Minor brusing or black eye: 13.8:10.1 b) Scratches: 10.8:5.4 c) Severe brusing or bleeding: 2.8:1.8 d) Mental/emotional problems: 48.4:49.3 e) Difficulty in other reelationships: 18.2:22.2 f) Tried to kill self: 6.5:2.8

How do I know these are not cherry picked studies?
In this grand study, Partner Abuse State of Knowledge(PASK) conducted by 42 scholars, 70 research assistants at 20 universities and research institutions over a course of two years involving 12k studies and summarising 1700 of them in tables, near gender symmetry was found. If any study has final say, this would be that.
Lifetime prevalence of partner abuse (victims): 23% women and 19.3% men. Perpetrators: 28.3% women and 21.6% men. Of the total violence: 57.9% were bidirectional, 28.3% unidirectional female to male and 13.8% unidirectional male to female. It also concluded that motives behind violence was similar for both genders: angry, jealousy, emotionally hurt, expressions that they could not convey verbally and to get their partner's attention. Thus analysis of an extreme volume of study still supports the symmetry. [https://domesticviolenceresearch.org/]
Meta study (343 studies) carried out by Prof. Martin Fiebert found women are as physically aggressive as men in their relationships with their spouses or opposite sex partners [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261543769_References_Examining_Assaults_by_Women_on_Their_Spouses_or_Male_Partners_An_Updated_Annotated_Bibliography]
Meta study (200+ studies) carried out by Prof. Murray Straus, found gender symmetry in perpetrators and in risk factors and motives for physical violence in martial and dating relationship. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233717660_Thirty_Years_of_Denying_the_Evidence_on_Gender_Symmetry_in_Partner_Violence_Implications_for_Prevention_and_Treatment]
Meta study (272 data sets) carried out by Prof. Sarah Desmarais found 28.3% of women and 21.6% of men reported perpetrating physical violence in an intimate relationship. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/233578820_Prevalence_of_Physical_Violence_in_Intimate_Relationships_Part_2_Rates_of_Male_and_Female_Perpetration]

Why don't men help themselves, are they afraid of their abusers?
26% of abuse men were still in abusive relationships. 81% of male victims told others of their abuse. 75% of male survivors were afraid of their (ex) partner. [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Jv5aBaZe_4&ab_channel=AnEarforMen]

cat.name: Scope & Coverage
cat.q: What is the geographic coverage of the legal policy database? Currently, the database maintains comprehensive coverage across North America, the European Union, the UK, and Australia. We are actively expanding our scope to include rigorous legal analyses and policy frameworks from South Asia and Latin America, collaborating with regional academic institutions to ensure translation and contextual accuracy.

Does the archive track historical trends or only current data? The archive prioritizes longitudinal data to establish historical context. Where available, statistical models extend back to 1990 to provide researchers with robust datasets capable of identifying long-term sociological and legislative trends.

cat.name: Editorial Process
cat.q: What constitutes the peer-review process for independent submissions? Independent submissions undergo a double-blind peer review by at least two domain experts from our academic advisory board. The review focuses strictly on methodological integrity, absence of ideological bias, and reproducible data practices. Submissions failing to meet academic publishing standards are rejected.
